questions.stem: Psychologists generally agree that every emotion is made up of which three components?
options: physiological responses, subjective feelings and expressive behaviour
facial expressions, body posture and tone of voice
arousal, attention and motivation to act on a goal
thoughts about the situation, long-term memories and personality traits
questions.explanation: An emotion combines bodily changes (such as a racing heart), a private felt experience, and outward behaviour that communicates the emotion to others. Facial expression, posture and voice are all parts of just one component, expressive behaviour.

questions.stem: Tom learns he has been picked for the state basketball team. His heart races, he feels elated, and he punches the air with a huge grin. Which part of his response is the expressive behaviour component?
options: his heart starting to race
his feeling of being elated
his memory of earlier team selections
punching the air with a huge grin
questions.explanation: Expressive behaviour is the observable action that communicates an emotion, such as a facial expression or gesture. The racing heart is a physiological response and elation is the subjective feeling.

questions.stem: According to the James-Lange theory, what is the order of events in an emotional experience?
options: stimulus, emotion, bodily changes, perception of those changes
stimulus, appraisal of its meaning, bodily changes, emotion
stimulus, emotion and bodily changes occurring at the same time
stimulus, bodily changes, perception of those changes, emotion
questions.explanation: James and Lange proposed that a stimulus first triggers physiological changes, and the emotion is our perception of those changes: we feel afraid because we tremble. Bodily changes and emotion happening at the same time is the Cannon-Bard view.

questions.stem: A driver swerves to miss a kangaroo. At the same instant, his heart pounds and he feels terror, and neither seems to cause the other. Which theory best describes this?
options: Lazarus' cognitive-mediational theory
Cannon-Bard theory
James-Lange theory
Schachter-Singer two-factor theory
questions.explanation: The Cannon-Bard theory holds that the physiological response and the felt emotion occur simultaneously and independently. The James-Lange theory would say the pounding heart came first and caused the terror.

questions.stem: In early studies, many people injected with adrenaline felt their heart race but said they felt only 'as if' they were afraid, without any real emotion. Which theory does this finding most directly challenge?
options: James-Lange theory, because bodily arousal alone did not produce emotion
Cannon-Bard theory, because arousal and the feeling occurred at the same time
Plutchik's theory, because fear is one of the eight primary emotions
Lazarus' theory, because participants appraised the injection first
questions.explanation: If emotion were simply the perception of bodily changes, artificially produced arousal should create a genuine emotion. Cannon used findings like this against the James-Lange theory. The finding fits the two-factor view that arousal needs a cognitive label to become an emotion.

questions.stem: What does the Schachter-Singer two-factor theory say is needed for an emotion to be felt?
options: an appraisal of a situation that comes before any arousal
physiological arousal plus a cognitive label that explains it
a stimulus that is relayed by the thalamus to the cortex
the perception of bodily changes without any thinking involved
questions.explanation: The two factors are general arousal and the cognitive interpretation of why we are aroused. The emotion depends on the label we give the arousal, so the same arousal could be felt as fear or excitement.

questions.stem: In Dutton and Aron's 1974 study, men interviewed by a woman on a high, swaying suspension bridge were more likely to phone her later than men interviewed on a low, stable bridge. Which explanation fits the two-factor theory?
options: the men's thalamus produced attraction and arousal independently
the men judged the interviewer to be a threat to their wellbeing
the men perceived calm bodily changes and so felt more relaxed
the men misattributed arousal caused by the bridge to attraction
questions.explanation: The high bridge produced arousal, and some men appear to have labelled that arousal as attraction to the interviewer. This misattribution of arousal is a key prediction of the two-factor theory, where the label, not the arousal itself, determines the emotion.

questions.stem: In Lazarus' cognitive-mediational theory, primary appraisal involves judging:
options: how other people around you are reacting to the same situation
whether a situation matters to your wellbeing and is a threat
whether you have the skills and support needed to cope with a situation
which label best explains the physical arousal you are already feeling
questions.explanation: In primary appraisal a person evaluates whether a situation matters to them and whether it is harmful, threatening or challenging. Judging whether you can cope is secondary appraisal.

questions.stem: Before a job interview, Kai thinks, 'I've practised my answers and my teacher gave me some tips, so I can handle this.' In Lazarus' theory, this thought is an example of:
options: cognitive labelling of arousal
perception of bodily feedback
secondary appraisal
primary appraisal
questions.explanation: Secondary appraisal is the evaluation of one's resources and options for coping. Kai has already recognised the interview as important, which is primary appraisal, and is now judging his ability to cope with it.

questions.stem: Mira hears a loud bang. Before her heart rate rises, she judges it to be a firework, so she feels mild surprise rather than fear. Which theory best fits the idea that her judgement came first and shaped her response?
options: Lazarus' cognitive-mediational theory
the Schachter-Singer two-factor theory
the James-Lange theory
the Cannon-Bard theory
questions.explanation: Lazarus argued that appraisal of a situation comes before, and determines, both the emotion and the physiological response. In the two-factor theory, arousal comes first and is then labelled, which does not fit a judgement made before any arousal.

questions.stem: According to Plutchik's wheel of emotions, how many primary emotions are there?
options: eight
six
seven
ten
questions.explanation: Plutchik proposed eight primary emotions: joy, trust, fear, surprise, sadness, disgust, anger and anticipation. Six is the number of basic emotions in Ekman's work on facial expressions, which is a different model.

questions.stem: Which pair of emotions are placed opposite each other on Plutchik's wheel?
options: anger and disgust
joy and sadness
joy and trust
fear and surprise
questions.explanation: The wheel arranges primary emotions in four opposing pairs: joy and sadness, trust and disgust, fear and anger, and surprise and anticipation. Joy and trust are neighbours, which is why they can blend into a combined emotion.

questions.stem: On Plutchik's wheel, annoyance, anger and rage differ mainly in their:
options: limbic structure
number of components
intensity
cultural origin
questions.explanation: The wheel shows intensity by distance from the centre: emotions become stronger towards the middle, so rage is the most intense form of anger and annoyance the mildest. All three belong to the same primary emotion.

questions.stem: In Plutchik's model, love is a blend of which two adjacent primary emotions?
options: fear and surprise
joy and trust
joy and anticipation
trust and fear
questions.explanation: Plutchik described more complex emotions as blends of neighbouring primary emotions: joy and trust combine as love. Joy and anticipation combine as optimism, and trust and fear as submission.

questions.stem: Which statement best compares the James-Lange and Cannon-Bard theories?
options: James-Lange says the feeling causes arousal; Cannon-Bard says arousal comes first
Both theories say a cognitive label is needed before any emotion is felt
Both theories say an appraisal of the situation comes before arousal
James-Lange says arousal causes the feeling; Cannon-Bard says both arise together
questions.explanation: In the James-Lange theory the felt emotion is the perception of bodily changes, so arousal comes first. Cannon-Bard rejected this, proposing that the thalamus triggers the feeling and the arousal at the same time. Neither theory gives cognition the central role that the two-factor and Lazarus theories do.

questions.stem: Which list contains only the main structures of the limbic system involved in emotional processing?
options: hypothalamus, thalamus, amygdala and hippocampus
hypothalamus, cerebellum, amygdala and medulla
thalamus, occipital lobe, pons and hippocampus
amygdala, cerebellum, pons and motor cortex
questions.explanation: The hypothalamus, thalamus, amygdala and hippocampus each play a role in emotion. The cerebellum, medulla, pons and occipital lobe are not part of the limbic system.

questions.stem: A bushwalker sees a snake on the track. Which limbic structure activates the sympathetic nervous system and signals the pituitary gland, preparing her body to respond?
options: corpus callosum
hypothalamus
hippocampus
thalamus
questions.explanation: The hypothalamus links the brain to the body, controlling the autonomic nervous system and, through the pituitary gland, the release of stress hormones. The thalamus relays sensory information but does not directly control these bodily responses.

questions.stem: Monkeys with damage to both amygdalae have been observed approaching snakes they would normally avoid. What does this suggest about the amygdala?
options: it forms new conscious memories of everyday events
it controls the release of hormones from the pituitary
it is involved in detecting threats and producing fear
it relays all incoming sensory information to the cortex
questions.explanation: Losing normal caution towards a dangerous stimulus suggests the amygdala is needed to recognise threat and trigger fear. Relaying sensory information is the role of the thalamus, and forming conscious memories is mainly the hippocampus.

questions.stem: A patient with hippocampal damage sweats when she sees a coloured card previously paired with a loud noise, yet cannot say which card was paired with it. A patient with amygdala damage shows the reverse. What does this suggest?
options: the amygdala stores the fear response; the hippocampus stores the conscious memory
the hippocampus stores the fear response; the amygdala stores the conscious memory
both structures store the same information, so either one can replace the other
neither structure is involved, because fear learning happens in the cerebellum
questions.explanation: The patient without a working hippocampus still learned the emotional response, but not the facts of the event; the patient without a working amygdala knew the facts but showed no fear response. This double dissociation suggests the amygdala handles emotional learning and the hippocampus conscious memory of the event.

questions.stem: LeDoux described a fast pathway carrying sensory information from the thalamus directly to the amygdala. What is the main advantage of this pathway?
options: it stops the sympathetic nervous system from responding to harmless stimuli
it triggers a fear response before the cortex has fully identified the stimulus
it allows a careful, detailed analysis of the stimulus before any response
it stores a conscious memory of the event in the hippocampus for later use
questions.explanation: The direct thalamus-to-amygdala route is quick but crude, so we can react to possible danger, such as a stick that looks like a snake, before conscious identification. The slower route through the cortex then gives a detailed analysis and can switch the fear off.

questions.stem: Cultural display rules are:
options: inborn facial movements that express the same emotion everywhere
laws that govern how emotions may be portrayed in advertising
the stages a person passes through when appraising an event
norms about when, where and how it is acceptable to show emotions
questions.explanation: Display rules are learned cultural norms that shape how emotions are expressed in different social settings. The facial movements themselves for basic emotions appear to be largely universal; display rules govern whether and how they are shown.

questions.stem: At funerals in some cultures, loud wailing is expected, while in others mourners are expected to stay quiet and composed. What does this best illustrate?
options: grief is felt only in cultures where people wail at funerals
facial expressions of sadness are learned entirely from culture
people in quieter cultures experience less physiological arousal
grief is shared, but display rules shape how it is expressed
questions.explanation: Mourners in both cultures experience grief, but their culture's display rules shape how openly it is shown. This does not mean the underlying emotion or facial expressions are entirely learned.

questions.stem: Studies at the Paralympic Games found that judo competitors who were born blind made the same spontaneous facial expressions after winning or losing as sighted athletes. Why is this important?
options: they could not have learned the expressions by seeing others, which suggests a biological basis
it shows that facial expressions are learned only through touch and hearing
it proves that culture has no effect on how people show any of their emotions
it shows that blind athletes feel stronger emotions than sighted athletes do
questions.explanation: People born blind have never seen a face, so producing the same expressions as sighted people suggests these expressions are innate rather than learned by imitation. Culture can still shape when expressions are shown, so it does not prove culture has no effect.

questions.stem: A student argues, 'Facial expressions are universal, so emotions mean the same thing in every culture.' Which response best fits the evidence?
options: only emotions with no facial expression, such as trust, are affected by culture in any way
expressions are universal only among people who share the same language and media
producing and recognising basic expressions seems universal, but their meaning and display are shaped by culture
recognising expressions differs completely between cultures, so no expression has a shared meaning
questions.explanation: People across cultures recognise and produce the basic facial expressions at rates well above chance, which supports universality. However, culture shapes when they are shown and what they signify; a smile, for example, can be used to mask embarrassment in some settings.

questions.stem: Emotional regulation refers to:
options: the ways people influence which emotions they have and how they express them
the automatic release of hormones by the pituitary gland during arousal
the cultural rules that decide which emotions are universally recognised
the process of diagnosing an emotional disorder using set criteria
questions.explanation: Emotional regulation includes strategies such as changing how we think about a situation, shifting attention, or controlling expression. It is something a person does, not an automatic hormonal process.

questions.stem: A classmate makes a rude comment. Jess tells herself he is probably stressed about exams, and her anger fades. Which emotional regulation strategy has she used?
options: cognitive reappraisal
expressive suppression
situation selection
physiological arousal
questions.explanation: Reappraisal changes how a situation is interpreted, which changes the emotion itself. Suppression would mean hiding the outward signs of anger while still feeling it.

questions.stem: In laboratory studies, participants told to hide their feelings while watching an upsetting film were compared with participants who watched normally. Which finding is typical?
options: suppression reduced visible expression but not the felt emotion, and raised arousal
suppression reduced the felt emotion and lowered arousal more than reappraisal did
suppression had no effect on visible expression but greatly reduced the felt emotion
suppression stopped all three components of emotion from occurring during the film
questions.explanation: Hiding an emotion reduces what others can see, but people still report feeling it, and their sympathetic arousal often rises. This is why reappraisal is generally considered a healthier regulation strategy than suppression.

questions.stem: A driver who is cut off in traffic tailgates the other car and shouts abuse out the window. Psychologically, this is best described as:
options: an example of cognitive reappraisal that reduces anger in a safe way
a primary emotion on Plutchik's wheel that cannot be controlled at all
a failure of emotional regulation that turns anger into dangerous behaviour
a cultural display rule that requires drivers to express anger openly
questions.explanation: Road rage occurs when anger is not regulated and is expressed through aggressive, risky behaviour. Reappraisal, such as assuming the other driver made an honest mistake, would reduce the anger rather than express it.

questions.stem: False news stories often use headlines designed to provoke outrage. Why does this help them spread on social media?
options: strong emotions make readers remember the source more accurately later
high-arousal emotions such as anger increase sharing and reduce careful checking
outrage makes readers more likely to check a story against reliable sources
angry readers usually scroll past stories quickly without reacting to them
questions.explanation: Emotionally arousing content tends to be shared more, and strong emotion can lead people to react before thinking critically about accuracy. Outrage therefore works against, not for, careful fact-checking.

questions.stem: Before an exam, Lucy plays a calming playlist on her phone to settle her nerves. This best illustrates:
options: technology being used as a device to regulate emotion
a cultural display rule about showing anxiety at school
the James-Lange theory, because the music caused arousal
an emotional disorder caused by too much screen time
questions.explanation: Lucy is deliberately using technology to change her emotional state, reducing anxiety. Technology and social networks can affect emotions both positively, as here, and negatively, such as through online conflict.

questions.stem: Emotional disorders are said to occur when:
options: a person shows the same facial expressions as people from another culture
a person's limbic system produces physiological responses during stress
difficulty regulating emotions becomes a problem or a danger to oneself or others
a person experiences any strong emotion, such as fear, for more than a few minutes
questions.explanation: Everyone experiences strong emotions, and arousal during stress is normal. An emotional disorder involves ongoing difficulty regulating emotions to the point where it causes significant problems or risk.

questions.stem: Over several months, Ben has had sudden, unexpected episodes of intense fear with a pounding heart and shortness of breath, and he now worries constantly about having another one. This pattern is most typical of:
options: a specific phobia
bipolar disorder
obsessive-compulsive disorder
panic disorder
questions.explanation: Panic disorder involves recurrent, unexpected panic attacks and persistent worry about further attacks. In a specific phobia, fear is triggered by a particular object or situation rather than coming unexpectedly.

questions.stem: Ana has intrusive, unwanted thoughts that her hands are contaminated, and she feels driven to wash them many times an hour to reduce her anxiety. Which disorder does this describe?
options: post-traumatic stress disorder
obsessive-compulsive disorder
panic disorder
bipolar disorder
questions.explanation: OCD involves obsessions (intrusive, distressing thoughts) and compulsions (repetitive behaviours performed to reduce the anxiety). The washing relieves anxiety briefly, which helps keep the cycle going.

questions.stem: Which feature distinguishes bipolar disorder from depression?
options: an intense fear of one specific object, such as spiders or heights
intrusive thoughts that lead to repeated checking or washing
episodes of mania, with elevated mood and high energy, plus depression
a persistent low mood that lasts most of the day for at least two weeks
questions.explanation: Bipolar disorder involves episodes of mania, with elevated or irritable mood, high energy and reduced need for sleep, alongside episodes of depression. A persistent low mood on its own is typical of depression.

questions.stem: An anger-management program would most likely teach participants to:
options: express anger immediately and loudly so that it does not build up inside
notice their triggers and early bodily signs, then use strategies like time out
suppress every outward sign of anger while continuing to feel it strongly
avoid all situations involving other people so anger can never be triggered
questions.explanation: Anger-management programs help people recognise what sets off their anger and the early physiological signs, then use regulation strategies such as time out, calming breathing and reappraisal. Suppression and venting tend not to reduce anger.

questions.stem: A researcher measures fear by recording participants' skin conductance (sweating) while they watch a horror film clip. This measure is best described as:
options: objective and qualitative
subjective and qualitative
objective and quantitative
subjective and quantitative
questions.explanation: Skin conductance is recorded by an instrument rather than judged by the participant, so it is objective, and it produces numbers, so it is quantitative. A participant's own fear rating would be subjective.

questions.stem: After a film clip, participants rate how sad they feel on a scale from 1 to 10, then describe their feelings in their own words. How are these two measures classified?
options: both measures are objective, because the participants report them truthfully
the rating is subjective and quantitative; the description is subjective and qualitative
the rating is objective and quantitative; the description is subjective and qualitative
the rating is subjective and qualitative; the description is objective and quantitative
questions.explanation: Both measures depend on the participant's own report, so both are subjective. The rating gives a number (quantitative), while the description is in words (qualitative).

questions.stem: A researcher video-records toddlers in a childcare centre and codes their facial expressions when a parent leaves, without changing anything about the setting. This is:
options: a qualitative investigation using a focus group
a Delphi technique investigation
an observational investigation
an experimental investigation
questions.explanation: The researcher collects data in a natural setting without manipulating an independent variable, which makes it observational. An experimental investigation would require the researcher to deliberately change a variable.

questions.stem: A researcher wants to interview people who were recently bereaved about their grief. Why do these participants need extra ethical protection?
options: they must be deceived about the study's aims to prevent biased answers
they may be vulnerable, so distress must be minimised and support offered
they cannot legally give consent until a full year has passed since the death
their emotions are too subjective for any data from them to be valid
questions.explanation: People experiencing extreme emotion can be classified as vulnerable. The researcher must make participation genuinely voluntary, minimise distress, make withdrawal easy, and provide access to support such as counselling.

questions.stem: In an experiment, participants are shown a sad film clip to induce mild sadness before a memory test. Which feature best justifies the study ethically?
options: participants who leave early are asked to explain why before they may go
the sadness is mild and brief, consent is informed and there is a debrief
the sadness is real, so the results will be more valid than in other studies
participants are not told about the clip, so they cannot avoid feeling sad
questions.explanation: Inducing emotion can be ethical when the effect is mild and temporary, participants know what is involved and agree, can withdraw at any time without explanation, and are debriefed afterwards. Requiring an explanation to withdraw would breach participants' rights.
